utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you again that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And I suppose Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May peace be in this house. I would like to welcome everybody, including General Nicolai, and may God's will be done and not mine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we discussed the smuggling of goods in Srebrenica and people who were discussed in that smuggling. However, we failed to arrive at any conclusions during that discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court please produce P620.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor tendered this document through you and the document is dated 4 July 1995. It's Karremans' report about the worsening of the situation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please produce page 2 for the witness and can we also look at paragraph 6, line 10 in the English language. And it is also page 2, line 6 in the Serbian version. We can see both versions on the screen -- or rather, both pages are in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sure that you will be able to read it in English. I don't have the Serbian version. In any case, it's page 2, paragraph 2, line 6. We are interested in the smuggling channels which have been closed. This is a letter dated 4 July. You spoke about this document in examination-in-chief, and the only thing that I'm interested here is this term "smuggling channels." Could you please tell us what smuggling channels are referred to herein?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think you will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Two things. Good morning, Mr. President. First, it's a communication dated 4 June 1995, just so we get ourselves orientated correctly. And I think General Tolimir called out paragraph 6 in the English, and if that's correct then we've just got it up on the B/C/S and it is on the English version, but I'm not sure if that's the paragraph he's interested in. But we do now have both correct versions on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you confirm that this number 6 is the paragraph you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct. I called out paragraph 6, line 10 in English, and in Serbian it is paragraph 6, line 7, where it says: "Smuggling routes have been closed." This is what I'm reading. If General Nicolai sees that in English in the sixth paragraph, maybe he can confirm whether he can see the paragraph where it says the "smuggling routes have been closed." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have little to add to this. This is an announcement that I simply accepted in light of the announcements in this report. This one did not strike me the most and I can't elaborate on it. I believe that Colonel Karremans or his deputy would be more able.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicolai. Have these documents been introduced through you and on examination-in-chief did you indeed say things about smuggling routes; if that is the case, then we can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this document was submitted by the Defence, but the report was drafted by Colonel Karremans. I'm familiar with the report but I have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court please produce P607, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a statement by a member of Dutch Battalion, Mr. Franken. You can see the English version at the moment, page 1. Can we also look at the Serbian version, also page 1, and can we also look at page 2 of his statement in Serbian, paragraphs 4 and 5. And in the English version it's the last paragraph on page 1 and the first paragraph on page 2. And I'm reading. The fourth paragraph of the Serbian version says: "During that time Serbs suggested that they should trade with Muslims at the prices that prevailed on the black market. When I say 'trade' I mean trade in everything except weapons. After several rounds of negotiations, the civilian authorities in the enclave allowed the Serbs to supply the enclave ... and the goods were being sold in the enclave at prices lower than the market prices and the DutchBat did not play any commercial role in this. "This filled in well with the vision that we had in our attempts to normalise relations between the warring factions. Rumours spread that the initiative was not viewed well by the groups that controlled the black market. The business was stopped by the military leadership. It was said by the local military leadership that the prohibition had come from the top of the military leadership, although such things worked well in Gorazde, and I presume that the initiative to boycott the business had really come from the military leadership of the enclave." My question to you is this: Did you receive reports about things mentioned by Mr. Franken in this statement of his? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any reports about that, but that there was trading between local Serbs and Muslims does not truly surprise me and that people trading on the black market ran into problems is perfectly understandable to me. But otherwise, these matters were not so important that they needed to be reported to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you receive reports about those groups which controlled the black market in the Srebrenica enclave, in view of the fact that your battalion was there and that you had special relations with that battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any reports about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the Popovic case on page 18458, lines 15 through 24, you said the following, and I quote you: "I did not have any formal direct contacts with the commander of the DutchBat because there was a level between the two of us. Strictly speaking, I was supposed to communicate with them through the staff in Tuzla. On the other hand, given the fact that I was the highest-ranking Dutch officer in the command, I was authorised to contact directly with my fellow citizens and I did that. I had a direct line of communication and I regularly informed myself about the situation, especially when things didn't go well. And obviously I contacted the commander of the DutchBat more often in order to inform myself about problems." My question to you is this: Who was that person in Srebrenica with whom you were mostly in contact with?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be clear, with the DutchBat commander, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you think that the information you received from the Dutch Battalion and the staff in Tuzla, either orally or verbally, was absolutely identical and reflected the real situation on the ground? Thank you. Or do you expect that there were discrepancies and that in view of the fact that you had personal contacts in addition to the official ones?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I've learned one thing from my time in Bosnia it's that things are not always the same in reality as they may initially appear to be, but I am not trying to suggest that Colonel Karremans deliberately provided me with inaccurate information or information other than what he sent me via the official reports, by the headquarters in Tuzla. So I assume that what he told me was the truth, or in any case, what he regarded as being the truth. To give you an example of things that are sometimes different than they appear to be, during the period that Sarajevo was surrounded and no supplies were coming in, the UN tried to supply the city from the air. And when there was shooting at such an aircraft, you would assume that it was being done by the units surrounding Sarajevo, the Serbs, but that was not always the case. Sometimes the shooting came from Muslims, purely because if too many goods came in, then the price would drop on the black market. And there were people in Sarajevo who benefited from a few supplies arriving. This is an example to indicate that things are not always the way you might at first think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have to stop here. There is a problem with the transcript. It stopped at page 6, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I formed the impression that everything is okay now. Then, sir, could you please look at the screen. You said: "So I assume that what he told me was ..." and then nothing else on the screen but it was quite important what you told us about aircraft supply for the population. Please repeat that for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat my statement. I was regularly in touch with Colonel Karremans, who would tell me about the situation in the enclave. I assume that what he told me was the reality or, in any case, what he perceived as the reality and did not deviate from what he communicated to the headquarters in Sarajevo via the official reports up to the headquarters in Tuzla. But I'll add - and this is what I learned in Bosnia - that things are not always as they initially appear to be. So it's perfectly possible that the reality that Colonel Karremans perceived deviated from what was actually happening and I'll give you an example to illustrate that. In the period that Sarajevo was surrounded and the supplies were cut off, the UN tried to supply the city from the air. Sometimes the aircrafts were shot at and the first idea you would think of is that the troops surrounding the city were doing this, so the Serbs. But in reality, this also happened by the Muslims purely because they had an interest in not having too many goods enter because otherwise the prices on the black market would drop too much. So when you observe something, you have to investigate very thoroughly what is actually happening because sometimes the reality is just slightly different than it appears to be. So it's perfectly possible that Colonel Karremans told me things sometimes, assuming that they were correct, but that might have differed from the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I apologise that you had to repeat your answer twice. At the end of session before the recess, you denied that you ever saw a report on the vehicles that were stolen and smuggled from Zepa through Srebrenica. On page 3955, line 24, through line -- 3956, you say: "I never received a report about APCs of the United Nations from Zepa. It sounds totally incredible to me in view of the fact that the enclave was completely encircled by Bosnian Serbs. I really can't imagine how they could have reached the Srebrenica enclave or how those APCs could have ended up in the hands of the Muslim forces. I really can't imagine how that could have been possible." Based on what you have said, I would like to read to you one part of Franken's testimony here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce the transcript from Franken's testimony of the 1st July 2010, page 3459, and on the other side can we see document 1D207. We don't see it on the screen yet. When we do see it, when paragraph 1 of this reconstruction of the interview with Franken was shown in the courtroom and when Mr. Franken was asked to comment, on page 3450, lines 14 through 19, Franken said, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it would be helpful if you could wait that we have it on the screen, then we can immediately follow what you are quoting from. Just a short moment that we have both documents on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3450, can we see it and display lines from 14 to 19. All I can see here is lines 21 to 25 -- no, no, it's okay. I apologise. 3450. No, it's not okay. No. Now we can see it. Thank you. Lines 14 through 19, and I quote: "... smuggled through the north not through the south, of course. And I saw the logistics report of the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa, because this is the information that we received from the UN" -- Because of the comment and the exchange between myself and my legal assistant, the page should be 3459, not 3450, and that will allow us to follow what I'm reading, lines from 14 to 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I will quote again. "... allegedly through the north but through the south, of course. And I saw that the Ukrainian unit in Zepa, in a logistics report, because that's the kind of information we got from the UN, reported the missing of five armoured personnel carriers." And then on page 3461, lines 8 through 9, 3461, lines 8 through 9, Mr. Franken says, and I quote: "My observation post saw them entering the enclave through the southern border." Thank you. And based on what I have just read, I would like to put several questions to you, sir. First of all, do you perhaps remember now that the Dutch Battalion reported to you that the observation post in the south of the enclave saw two APCs that had entered the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I still don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that you weren't informed about this, the topic that Mr. Franken testified about here and the portion I quoted from the transcript? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds like the most likely explanation to me. If it's about something so important as UN vehicles that are not part of DutchBat entering the enclave, then that incident would be so important you would never forget about that. So had that been reported, then I would undoubtedly still remember that to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But are these Mr. Franken's words, because I quoted them directly from the transcript? Is that what he said in his testimony? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've not objected up to this point just because it would be too time-consuming, I think, to break it up and I think the General is capable of answering the questions as they've been put, but I think we all know the background to General Tolimir's examination of Mr. Franken, what Colonel Franken had to say about this reconstructed transcript. Now we're at the point where General Tolimir is asking General Nicolai to comment on what Colonel Franken said before this Trial Chamber a couple of months ago, and, number one, I submit that that's not helpful to anybody to have General Nicolai tell the Court whether or not these are Colonel Franken's words. And if he is going to ask that question, then he needs, I think, to show General Nicolai all of Colonel Franken's words, for example, where Colonel Franken says at 3461, line 10: "I didn't get exactly when, in what period or where those large number of vehicles, UN vehicles, were seen. Is that referring to the Srebrenica area or any other area? "Then again, we only saw two and never saw them again, but if you ask me if anything is possible, I can confirm that." That's just one example of Colonel Franken's words on this topic that General Tolimir did not put before General Nicolai. And if he's going to ask these kinds of questions, I think he needs to show General Nicolai all of the related testimony from Colonel Franken. I don't think that's fruitful, so I, frankly, think we should move on. Unless there are more focused, particular questions, then we have no objection to this line of questioning as such. It's just this last line, I think, is not going to be very helpful for anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, about the concerns of the Prosecution, I would recommend that you ask about facts and not about the words in the transcript. Everybody can read the transcript of a previous testimony of another witness. If -- of course this witness today is not in the position to confirm that Mr. Franken said, really said, this what is recorded on the transcript. We have on the transcript and that's all. Please ask questions related to the facts you want to know. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, General, sir, is it a fact that the officers of your battalion in Srebrenica say that they saw two APCs coming into the enclave from the south which did not belong to the United Nations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said earlier. It was never reported to me that UN vehicles not pertaining to DutchBat entered the enclave, so I can't elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have the answer and that -- I've got no objection to, I think, what General Tolimir was asking, but the question he asked does not reflect even what's in the transcript. I think to the extent that Colonel Franken testified about some UN DutchBat soldiers seeing APCs, I think the testimony was clear that those APCs did have UN markings. And the question that -- General Tolimir, I think that's reflected in LiveNote, is that they did not have UN markings. So I just -- you know, the issue is becoming less clear the further we're going on and I just want to make that clear. I don't know if that was just simply General Tolimir misspeaking, but I think the evidence is clear from the record what Colonel Franken reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think this way of dealing with the kind of questioning should be out of your re-examination. I think according to my recommendation Mr. Tolimir asked about facts and not related to the testimony of Mr. Franken. I think we should continue -- Mr. Tolimir should continue, and then you are in a position to deal with it in re-examination. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, sir, did you ever receive or see or hear about a logistics report in which it was stated that the Krajina people needed five APCs more and that this information was forwarded to the United Nations in the so-called position report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what this is about, but it doesn't sound like it has anything to do with what we were just talking about. So perhaps General Tolimir could clarify what this relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The United Nations, in their logistics reports, did they present the information reported by individual units and it was the Ukrainian Battalion that notified of the disappearance of the vehicle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not the Krajina people, Ukrainian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So is this the kind of information that would be forwarded once it is reported officially? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that seems obvious. Missing five vehicles that are moreover recognisable as UN vehicles is a serious incident and should certainly have been reported because the risk that the vehicles would be abused was very high and we should warn all units about this. But I never received such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question is this: Did you ever, from the Dutch Battalion in the reports and communications that you maintained regularly with them, did you ever ask them whether the BH Army in Srebrenica was arming itself illegally? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I did receive a report that they never succeeded fully in entirely disarming the Muslims within the enclave. They did manage to take receipt of their heavy arms and place them in storage, but if we're talking about smaller fire-arms, they're so easy to hide, it was never possible to seize all of those. And whether any weapons were smuggled in during the interim was not reported to me, but I don't consider it unlikely that that happened from time to time. Given the surroundings of Sarajevo, that's -- it's certainly not impossible to secretly smuggle weapons in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. For the Trial Chamber to understand this correctly and since you know the situation well and are best placed to tell me, tell me this: What was the relationship between the enclaves, or rather, the UN forces in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa? Since the BH Army relations were tied up in -- and Srebrenica, in Zepa and Srebrenica. So the Ukrainian Battalion, what was that linked to? And it was in control of Zepa. And what was the Dutch Battalion linked to, controlling Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there was no direct contact between the UN troops in the Zepa enclave and the DutchBat in Srebrenica. Both reported to their commanders, but as far as I know, there was never any direct contact between the two enclaves. But Karremans or Franken would be better able to answer those questions than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you tell us whether there were any proposals for the commands to be united, the command structures of the UNPROFOR forces in Zepa and Srebrenica, that they should be joined up, since the enclaves were next door to each other? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such proposal was ever made, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have 1D33 called up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's a document from the BH Army. It is Naser Oric's order dated the 19th of May, 1995, and in paragraph 1, which is the one I'd like us to focus on, it says - it hasn't come up on our screens yet so we'll just take a moment. It's up on the B/C/S in Serbian and you can see it now in English. It says in paragraph 1: "We have received intelligence from the Main Staff of the BH Army that members of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR might leave the area of responsibility of the 28th Division and that's Srebrenica and Zepa. "So we issue an order in relation to that." And the order is: "1. Prevent UNPROFOR members from leaving the zone of responsibility of the 28th Division in accordance with previous orders and plans for the prevention of their departure." You've been able to read point 1 there now. And here's my question relating to that: When this order was issued, and the date is the 19th of May, 1995, was there a plan whereby the members of the Dutch Battalion should leave Srebrenica enclave; and if such a plan did exist, what did it consist of? And did you look into the possibility of having DutchBat replaced by somebody else in Srebrenica in the month of May? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can't provide a brief answer to this, but I hope you'll give me the latitude to provide a detailed answer here. We need to distinguish a few things. In May 1995, the Dutch government already intended to end the mission in Srebrenica and the Dutch government was trying to find a country that would be willing to take over the duties in Srebrenica. The Dutch government had not succeeded yet in May, so specific plans as to which plan would replace the Netherlands in Srebrenica did not exist at that time. I don't think that the order displayed on the screen related to that. There were plans in case of an emergency to attempt to break out and to have DutchBat use violence to attempt to return to safe territory. If such a situation made it inevitable. For example, if there was a danger that the supplies would be completely exhausted, but in mid-May the situation did not yet justify this and it was not yet time for the emergency plan. That's why it's unclear to me what this order refers to. The supply situation in May was definitely cause for concern, though, and Colonel Karremans reported that he had trouble performing his duties, but the possibility of retreating from Srebrenica was not considered at that time, it wasn't relevant, and that was already discussed in previous questions. Even in early June when he said he couldn't perform his duties properly anymore, he insisted on continuing to have his observation posts manned. So abandoning his mission was never a point to him which the UN leadership in Sarajevo would have agreed, even if the UN leadership in Sarajevo had agreed to abandon the observation posts. So I certainly don't understand what this order refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I asked you and you answered. Now, may we have D70, page 8, of your statement called up on e-court, please, the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor. Now, on page 8 of that statement you talk about the consultations you had with NATO and that you prepared a plan for delivering supplies to the enclave. And I'm going to quote from that page once it comes up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8, please, the penultimate paragraph. And it's also on page 8 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Many problems developed from then on in trying to supply the enclaves. The VRS would only give permission for some of the convoys to proceed. Then they would block access to some of these convoys. I was asked by General Smith to prepare a more sophisticated plan to supply the enclaves. Some of the factors required to carry out such a plan were creating air routes, preparation for air cover and protection, to arrange for air refuelling planes, air rescue helicopters, and teams being made available. This plan was prepared together with much consultation with NATO. This plan was made known to the national governments of the troops and equipment involved, as it was not a normal peacekeeping action. This resulted in some governments not giving full permission for this course of action. This plan was never allowed to be put into effect." That's the whole paragraph and now my question is this. Since we can see that this plan involved the engagement of joint NATO and UNPROFOR resources, my question is: Was it a plan to prepare rapid intervention forces, generally speaking? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time UNPROFOR did not yet have rapid intervention capabilities, so that wasn't relevant yet. The rapid intervention capability was brought into Bosnia-Herzegovina only in late June 1995. So the only opportunity to deploy other means was by air and a plan was drafted for that purpose. And the plan was held intact, but upon execution would require the consent of the concerned countries and they were willing to grant such consent only if there was no other means of rescuing the troops in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you tell us which countries, as you say in the statement of yours, were opposed to the plan and which countries did not give full approval for acting in this way, and what did you mean by "full permission "? So which countries did not provide full permission and what do you mean by "full permission"?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "full permission," I mean unconditional permission, which means that those countries delegated full say over deployment of their air force to UNPROFOR. That's what they didn't want. The countries specifically concerned I can't tell you. Those negotiations were conducted from Zagreb and all I was told was that they had not succeeded in getting that commitment from the troop-supplying countries and that this would be negotiable only when the situation in the enclaves became so desperate that the survival of the troops was in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question is this: For the transcript can you tell us when the rapid intervention forces arrived in Bosnia and who was -- which was their first combat assignment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the rapid intervention troops arrived in June and the plans drafted for these intervention troops were basically -- they were still only in draft form, but some involved making access to the city of Sarajevo to enable supply and drafting a plan to enable a supply route to the enclaves. Those are two that I know about, but as you also know, having an idea of what you want to do with troops is one thing but elaborating a plan to make this feasible is the second thing and that's considerably more time-consuming. And I believe that in that period, especially early June 1995, those plans were not ready yet. I'd like to add something. One task that the intervention troops did carry out was bringing heavy weapons to Mount Igman. That's the mountain close to Sarajevo. And when I say "heavy weapons," I'm referring to artillery and mortars. And the purpose of those heavy weapons was to fight the heavy weapons by the Serbs when those were deployed against the Sarajevo population. That plan was carried out and in practice ultimately in August 1995 was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before August 1995 was the heavy weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska set aside under special -- and put under special control of UNPROFOR? And if that happened, was it during your mandate?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the heavy weapons of the Bosnian Serb republic? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's correct, General. And before that, were the heavy weapons collected from the Army of Republika Srpska and handed over to UNPROFOR to be safe-guarded at special points?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a brief answer to this either. Based on resolutions by the Security Council of the United Nations, the heavy weapons in the immediate surroundings of some of the enclaves, in any case the Sarajevo enclave, all heavy weapons located within a certain distance of that city considered to be a threat were gathered at what were known as weapon collection points and they were under UNPROFOR supervision. The troops were allowed to maintain their weapons, but UNPROFOR ensured that they were not used. And this concerned only the weapons within those immediate surroundings. Still, the Bosnian Serb republic did have heavy weapons that were not in the immediate surroundings of Sarajevo. So that was the situation at that point in time. And as for the other enclaves outside the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, there were no weapon collection points, so heavy weapons were still -- of the Bosnian Serb republic were still located around those enclaves and could still be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir was asking you about the heavy weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Bosnian Serb army. Now you were referring to the Bosnian Muslim, the BH army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, that's not correct. I specifically answered about the heavy weapons of the Bosnian Serbs. As for the heavy weapons of the Muslims, those were all in weapon collection points within the enclaves and under strict UNPROFOR supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my mistake. I misunderstood you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, let's clarify one thing. Was only Muslim weaponry under the supervision of UNPROFOR or was it also the weaponry belonging to the Bosnian Serbs in Sarajevo and within the 20-kilometre perimeter of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I just answered. The heavy weapons of the Bosnian Serbs within a radius of 20 kilometres of the city of Sarajevo were gathered in weapon collection points, and those were under UNPROFOR supervision. And I can illustrate this because the impetus for the air attacks conducted in late May at UNPROFOR's request were carried out because weapons of the Bosnian Serbs had disappeared from those weapon collection points and the UN set an ultimatum for the return and said that otherwise there would be air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we have clarified things and we understand that we are talking about the heavy weapons of the Army of Republika Srpska. You said clearly in your statement that the Army of Republika Srpska did not have any heavy weaponry in the vicinity of Sarajevo but it did have it in the vicinity of Zepa and Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partially correct. The last part is certainly right. Heavy weapons around Zepa and Srebrenica, pertaining to the Bosnian Serb -- Bosnian Serbs, were never gathered in weapons collections points. That was the case, that did happen around Sarajevo, but I never alleged that all heavy weapons of the Bosnian Serbs around Sarajevo were placed in the weapon collection points. And this is clear from the fact that despite the existence of weapon collection points, the city of Sarajevo was nonetheless often shot at by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please tell us, did the rapid intervention forces arrive in Bosnia with the consent of the Security Council and was there a resolution in place to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first is correct. Those forces arrived with permission from the UN, and that must mean that there was also a resolution about that. But the booklet I have listing Security Council Resolutions was presented to me before I travelled to Bosnia. So that resolution is obviously not listed there so I can't check, but I'm sure the Trial Chamber can verify that. I can't imagine that those forces were brought there without a Security Council Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you tell us, please, do you know whether there was resolution? Are you sure there was one? Or are you not? And I'm talking about the arrival of Rapid Reaction Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This question is already answered. There was a clear answer by the witness on that point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. However, in the transcript it says they did not come without the permission of the United Nations, but what I want to know whether there was a resolution in place to that effect. They could have been given permission by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. What I'm interested in is whether there was a resolution that preceded their arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, this question is already answered. The witness said that he doesn't know about that, but that then, I quote: "I can't imagine that those forces were brought there without a Security Council Resolution." But he doesn't know. Please carry on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, did you negotiate with the warring parties about the arrival of the Rapid Reaction Forces? If that was indeed the case, who did you negotiate with, or rather, who did you not negotiate with? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the last part of your question is the easiest to answer. There were no negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs. There were negotiations with the representatives of the BiH and with the government of the Bosnian part because those troops had to be placed on that -- in that area and that would require permission from the government in charge of that area. So we consulted with the government in Sarajevo as to where those troops should be placed and what the potential objectives might be of these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Does that mean that those forces were intended only for actions outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina where they were deployed, for example, actions against the HVO or the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was basically left up to UNPROFOR. The troops brought in were not presented with a specific objective. This even led General Smith to make a cynical remark, "Now I have even more mouths to feed." So it was basically left up to General Smith to determine what he wanted to use these troops for. And theoretically, they could also be used against the Muslims or against the Croatians; but given the situation at the time, deployment against the Bosnian Serbs was the most plausible option.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will continue discussing this topic. And now, since other witnesses have also dealt with the issues and some witnesses even said that you participated in those negotiations, I would like to announce our topic for tomorrow and I would like to ask you whether there were discussions about the deployment of Rapid Reaction Forces during the events in Srebrenica and Zepa. And were those forces actually deployed anywhere near those enclaves?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in negotiations about the deployment and placement of the Rapid Reaction Forces. There were also negotiations about displacing the heavy weapons of those forces to the surroundings of Sarajevo. In practice, those -- some of those heavy weapons were, in fact, transferred before the government in Sarajevo had granted permission for that, so we basically anticipated such permission because we urgently needed heavy weapons in the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were Rapid Reaction Forces located or deployed in the sector of Zepa; or to be more precise, on Boksanica hill and whether that was legal and whether they were closer to UNPROFOR in that way?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether the translation I received was entirely correct, but if the question is about whether the intervention forces were already deployed near the Zepa surroundings, the answer is no. We were still in the midst of examining deployment opportunities, and I've already answered that the only part of the Rapid Reaction Forces deployed were the artillery and mortars and they were deployed in the surroundings of Sarajevo from Mount Igman. And other -- in all other respects during my period there were only plans and nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We can continue discussing this topic tomorrow after you've had a thought. And now I would like to move on to agreements on demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce document D21, page 2. This is an agreement on demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document to appear on the screen, I have a question that has nothing to do with the document. Before you were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have an occasion to analyse the demilitarisation agreement that was signed in 1993 by the VRS and the Army of the Federation? And your troops were already in one of those zones, as we know. Thank you. Now we can see the provisions of the agreement on the demilitarisation that was signed by General Sefer Halilovic and Colonel Ratko Mladic and that was on the 8th of May, 1993. That agreement was in force until the expiry of the term of deployment of your troops in Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a problem to understand your question. Could you perhaps break up your long and different questions. At the end there is no question, only at the first part of your statement. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to familiarise yourself with the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica before assuming your duties in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the case. I learned about -- I first learned about this during the briefing from my predecessor, General Brinkman, and that was after I had arrived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, did you realise what the obligations of UNPROFOR was according to that agreement and what tasks did it have to perform during the deployment in the UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I've understood your question correctly, then the answer is as follows. The UN was responsible for ensuring that heavy weapons within a given distance of the city of Sarajevo so that they posed a threat, that they were stored in weapon collection points and that they would not be used by the parties who owned them. The troops did have permission to maintain their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce paragraph 5 in this agreement where it says -- we will see it in a minute, paragraph 5. And I quote from the paragraph -- I will actually quote from it when I see it on the screen. I don't see it yet. Now I do. "UNPROFOR shall control the demilitarised zone. "To be able to implement this, an UNPROFOR unit and UNMOs with sufficient strength to control the area shall be present in the demilitarised zone. Until the contracting parties agree otherwise, the UNPROFOR strength shall be of at least a company group with command and supplying elements in each demilitarised zone. "In order to be able to resupply and rotate the unit, UNPROFOR shall have freedom of movement to and from the demilitarised zone."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Did UNPROFOR have the freedom of movement as is stipulated here in Article 5? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the demilitarised zone around Sarajevo, that was the case until the end of May. After the incident in which heavy weapons were removed from the weapon collection points in the subsequent air-strikes, there was no more freedom of movement. In fact, the troops at the weapon collection points that were located, they were more or less held hostage by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My question was about the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa, so I was asking about Srebrenica. And let's do it once again and let's be very precise. Let's look at paragraph 4 and 5 -- or rather, Article 5 where it says: "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone except members of UNPROFOR are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition, and explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR." And paragraph 5 where it says: "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." Did you see that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. As far as I know, no demilitarised zone was ever accomplished in the surroundings of Sarajevo. There were no UNPROFOR troops outside the enclave and everywhere around the enclave Bosnian Serb troops were present and heavy weapons were located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm asking you about Srebrenica, because this demilitarisation agreement concerns Srebrenica which enjoyed the status of a demilitarised zone, unlike Sarajevo. I'm asking you about Srebrenica and my complete question is this: In Srebrenica were your troops, or rather, did the Dutch Battalion have any restrictions on movement in and around the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I just said. As far as I know, no demilitarised zone was ever realised around Srebrenica. Within the enclave, UNPROFOR had freedom of movement. Outside the enclave, this was not possible without permission from the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What you have just stated, does this mean that the zone was never demilitarised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's the case. In any case, it should be clear that for months, especially in June and July, the enclave was regularly shelled from outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was the impression in the media, both in Bosnia and in the United Nations, wrong about the zone being demilitarised, although, as you have just stated, there were people carrying weapons around Srebrenica contrary to the provisions of the agreement that I have just quoted from?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very clearly that there was a difference between demilitarised zones around Srebrenica and Sarajevo. I had a map of the surrounding of Sarajevo clearly indicating a border within which no heavy weapons were allowed except in weapon collection points, and I never saw such a map of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. This means that apparently the negotiations had yet to take place about that and that such a zone was never actually realised. And the only thing you could do up to that point was that the moment heavy weapons were used in the immediate surroundings of the enclaves, then we could have used air force against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please, in order to avoid any confusion we are now talking about Srebrenica and Zepa. We are no longer discussing the issue of Sarajevo. I have a document before me about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica which was signed by Halilovic and Mladic. And in the first paragraph that I see before me on the screen it says: "Non-combatants ..." And I'm quoting from paragraph 4 and 5 of Article 5. "Non-combatants who are in or who are willing to enter the demilitarised zone except members of UNPROFOR are not permitted to have in their possession any weapons, ammunition, or explosives. Weapons, ammunition or explosives in their possession shall be seized by UNPROFOR. "Combatants will not be allowed to enter or to be in the demilitarised zone." Do you see that in the English language? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was about that. Was that zone indeed ever demilitarised? If not, were you abreast of that situation? Were members within the zone disarmed by UNPROFOR or did they continue carrying weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the fighters within the enclave, then I can tell you that UNPROFOR relieved them of their heavy weapons, and I've said that earlier in this session. UNPROFOR never succeeded in obtaining all handguns and I said earlier that they're easy to conceal and it's difficult to ensure that they've all been seized. Outside the enclave we never managed to carry out this mission. So there were no weapon collection points outside the enclave in which heavy weapons of Bosnian Serbs were stored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we got this answer from the witness much earlier already. He discussed it several times the same, and you should focus on specific topics you are interested in. Otherwise, it's really a waste of time if you repetitively ask the same questions several times. Now we reach the point of the first break. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the outset of this session, I would like to mention in brief that we checked the legal situation about protective measures. And now we came to the conclusion that our Chamber is one Chamber of the second proceedings. There is no Chamber of third proceedings in our Rules. Pursuant to Rule 75(F)(i): "... protective measures shall have effect mutatis mutandis in any other proceedings before the Tribunal ..." Therefore, our recommendation is to file such an application, if you want to do that, related to protective measures for a certain witness before this Chamber. Mr. Tolimir, could you indicate when will you submit such an application? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If it's urgent then, with my signature, my assistant Aleksandar Gajic will send it by e-mail, with your permission, because we have agreed what it should contain rather than having the person coming in and so on. So if you grant permission, then we can use this -- we can do this by e-mail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this exceptional situation, I think there's no concern about that and we would like to receive an immediate response by the Prosecution so that we can deal with this problem immediately. Thank you very much. I think this is enough for the moment to this problematic matter and we shall continue with the examination of the witness. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, since you and I have discussed various topics up till now, we're now going to look at demilitarised zones. And the status of demilitarised zones according to an agreement between the warring sides were only two: Srebrenica and Zepa. Those were the only two zones that had the status of a demilitarised zone. Now, I would like you to tell me whether you received reports from your units about whether Zepa and Srebrenica were actually demilitarised zones or whether there were weapons there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is the third time I'm being asked this question. I've said previously that troops in the enclave were disarmed or in any case relieved of their heavy weapons. I can't guarantee that they were relieved of handguns. The heavy weapons around the enclave were never removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Tolimir. Just before the break I advised you that you shouldn't repeat this question again and again. Please carry on but with a new question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to ask the question for the transcript. I have to ask whether the General received reports and whether the zone was demilitarised or not. I can't get an answer yes or no. I'm not asking him about heavy weapons. That wasn't in the agreement, the one that I quoted and the one that General looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because if the Serb side, General, grants Srebrenica a demilitarised zone status --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. I'm very sorry, Mr. Tolimir. This is not an appropriate way. You have your questions on the transcript and you have the answers on the transcript several times and it's not necessary to have it a third or fourth or fifth time on the transcript. Please carry on, and not repeat the same question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I didn't ask whether the Army of Republika Srpska withdrew its heavy weapons around the zone which was given the status of a demilitarised zone. I haven't asked that yet and that's what I'm getting in the answer. So that's not the question. The question was whether the zone was demilitarised. So I'm repeating my question on the basis of your answers. The possession of light weapons by persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not acceptable. You have asked this question several times and you got the answer this witness is able to provide. You got an answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, General, the Muslim forces, were they in the demilitarised zone and disarmed? Were their light weapons taken away from them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the actual enclave all the heavy weapons were seized. I cannot guarantee that that was the case for the handguns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, do you know the contents of Article 60 of the Additional Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions which regulates the question of demilitarised zones and their status or do you wish me to read it out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know about demilitarised zones appears in the corresponding Security Council Resolutions. If I remember correctly, those are, for example, 824 and 836, which stipulate in any case that heavy weapons that were a threat to the enclaves concerned need to be at a sufficient distance so that they were no longer a threat to those enclaves or stored at weapon collection points under UNPROFOR's supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Does that refer to the protected areas or to the demilitarised zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers to the protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Srebrenica and Zepa, before the proclamation of the protected zones, did they -- were they given the status of demilitarised zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you see when the agreement was drawn up - and that was in 1993 we said earlier on - and what about the resolution on protected zones, when was that -- when did that come into force?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We'd have to check the dates of the relevant Security Council regulations [as interpreted]. I don't know that off the top of my head. They predate my arrival in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now tell me, please, whether when the measures were discussed that needed to be taken by UNPROFOR with respect to the attack on Srebrenica, did they take into account Article 7 -- Article 60, paragraph 7 of the Additional Protocol which states, and I quote: "If one of the Parties" -- so Article 60 in the Additional Protocol of 1977. If one party in the conflict makes a material infringement of the para 3 and 6, the other side will be free of its obligations in the area that has the status of demilitarised zone. So did you bear in mind what it says in Article 60 of the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols of 1977 on the protection of prisoners of war and so on?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this article, so I didn't take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have Exhibit P592. It's a report of the United Nations peace forces about the situation in the field from the -- and it's dated the 10th of July, 1995, and we're interested in page 14 of this document. It's paragraph 3 in Serbian and page 6, paragraph 3 of the English. Thank you. Let me repeat. Page 14 of the Serbian, paragraph 3, please, so not page 18 but page 13. And page 6 in English, paragraph 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're looking at paragraph 3 in the two versions, and I'm going to quote from it. "The Bosnian Serbs could halt their advance pending a number of conditions: The complete demilitarisation of the enclave will probably be their highest priority. This would also serve their primary goal of freeing troops from around the enclave for other purposes." Now, my question on the basis of this is the following: Did UNPROFOR consider this report, this UN peace forces report, and look at the option presented in this analysis, that is, the complete demilitarisation of Srebrenica in conformity with the agreement reached in 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just as a courtesy to the witness if General Tolimir is going to continue to ask him questions about this report, such as did the UN rely on the report, then I think the witness should be allowed to look at the report. If nothing else, look at the first page of the report so he knows what it is. We have no idea what it is -- we've all seen this with the prior witness, but I don't know if General Nicolai has ever been shown this before. So perhaps just a moment for the witness to familiarise himself with the report before he begins his answer would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a very helpful advice. Could we move to the first page, please. We need the second page. This seems to be a cover page. Mr. Nicolai, do you recall this report? Have you ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as far as I know. The report was drafted in Zagreb, so it is probably a report that was sent to New York. I see it's addressed to Mr. Annan. So this is not a report that was sent to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now we may continue and go back to the page we have seen earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness now be shown page 6, paragraph 3, and I would like to have page 14, paragraph 3 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to tell me now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I remember this document somewhat. I don't have it because it wasn't on the cross-examination list, but if my recollection is correct, the prior page to what's on here is actually the beginning of this section that General Nicolai is being asked about with -- it states what it is and what the source is. I think that page might be helpful for General Nicolai to see just because it's -- we're looking at a paragraph here and I think it starts on the other page. So it may be useful -- I can't remember whether it's a long passage or a short passage, but I remember that I think it starts on the prior page. I just simply ask that he be given an opportunity to see the section we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's go to the previous page. Perhaps one page back. Mr. Thayer, is this the page you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is -- as everybody can see, it's a long document, it's 14 pages because it's a report from various sectors, and the sector involving Srebrenica I think begins here with the section headed "Sector North East," and that's reporting on the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we should go back to the page Mr. Tolimir was asking for. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, can you tell us on the basis of which at the top command level documents of this kind are compiled and sent to the UN. Is it basis on -- based on the situation on the ground or on personal assessment, and this particular document what -- how was that drafted, on what basis and grounds? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports are drafted based on the reports from the sub-commanders. So if Sector South West issues an assessment, then they do this based on reports received from the troops under their command. So, for example, DutchBat in Srebrenica. On the one hand, you base it on events that took place; on the other hand, expectations are stated based on those events as to what the future course of events will be. So generally such reports start with a fact report of what took place and that's usually followed by an assessment of the subsequent course of events, so expectations of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read it out, but just tell me for the record whether UNPROFOR ever considered the possibility, based on this report as we've just read it out, about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica in conformity with the 1993 agreement, as it says in the paragraph that I've just put to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to emphasise again - I believe this is the fifth time - that as to the demilitarisation of the enclave, we managed to seize and store the heavy weapons in the enclave but did not succeed in doing so for the handguns. And given the minimal number of troops in the enclave at that time, that would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now let's take a look at the following: Page 14 of the Serbian and page -- and the same page in English. So page 14 in both Serbian and English, paragraph 6. Thank you. I see it in the Serbian and it reads as follows: "The pressure from the Army of Republika Srpska on the enclave will lead to increased movements of civilians to the already overcrowded urban areas. This will affect the relations between the local population and the UN forces. If the local authorities find that UNPROFOR is not doing enough to protect the enclave, retaliation against UN forces (blocking of compounds, harassment) can be expected." Now, my question on the basis of that is the following. This document was compiled on the 10th of July, as we saw on page 1. Can you tell us what the indices were, or rather, the -- what of this was included in the report that was sent to Kofi Annan? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood the question properly, but what this reads is that as a consequence of the pressure on the enclave, the local population in the enclave sought safety by fleeing to the cities or the villages in the areas, so towards the city of Srebrenica, which meant that the population was concentrated in a small area. And it was expected that if the UN did not manage to provide sufficient protection to the local population that they would retaliate to the UNPROFOR troops, for example, by blocking compounds or by impeding movement of troops, which did in fact happen once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was that UNPROFOR's obligation, to comply with the demands made by the Muslim side regardless of demilitarisation and the agreement which was in existence between the two warring parties? So did UNPROFOR in the enclave have to meet the requirements of the Muslim and local population?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think there may be some problems with the translation. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'll repeat the question. In this paragraph that you have just repeated speaks about a possible conflict between the local authorities and UNPROFOR. Did UNPROFOR avoid such conflicts by not enforcing the agreement on demilitarisation; or in other words, did UNPROFOR choose to leave the weapons in the possession of those people in order to avoid any conflicts with them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no. Until just before the fall -- until just before the fall of the enclave, UNPROFOR prevented Muslim troops from having heavy weapons at their disposal in the enclave. Regarding the light weapons, as I said, it was always our intention to disarm Muslim warriors within the enclave, but we were physically unable to do so, and the situation at the time described here was no different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The UNPROFOR command or UNPROFOR in the field, did they fear from Muslim local forces -- did they believe that Muslims might be able to attack UNPROFOR and take their positions in Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never feared that and it never became apparent that Muslim warriors intended to take over those positions. What we did fear was that out of dissatisfaction with the lack of protection provided by the UN troops, the Muslim warriors would impede the movements of the UNPROFOR troops within the enclave, and that happened, for example, on Saturday, 8 July. I'm familiar with an incident where a DutchBat soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was UNPROFOR's movement ever restricted by Muslims within the UN protection zones?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until the period concerned in early July, that was never a problem. It was only in the final days before the fall of the Srebrenica enclave that UNPROFOR was restricted, and this was because the Muslim soldiers wanted to try to stop DutchBat soldiers from leaving their observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know anything about the so-called problem of the triangle in Srebrenica and the way that problem was being dealt with? Was that something that was dealt with at your level by your command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about now or which triangle. I assume it's something that did not involve the headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'll try and introduce you to the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, can the court produce D66. Thank you. Thank you. We have it on the screen in the Serbian. Could the General please be provided with the English version. This report was drafted in January 1995, on the 28th of January, 1995, by Naser Oric, and in this report Naser Oric informs the command of the BiH army and the command of the 2nd Corps: "Due to the events which took place in Podgaj village section on 9 January 1995, of which you were informed in a timely measure, the command of the 8th Operation Group has restricted the movement of the UNPROFOR forces in the wider region of Suceska and Podgaj." So he's talking about the restriction of movement of UNPROFOR. "At about 1100 hours today, the commander of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica ordered his patrols to enter the movement restriction area. In co-ordination with the commander of the 8th Operation Group, respecting the agreement reached with the UNPROFOR liaison officer, after the warning was issued not to move in the aforementioned area, the commander of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade blocked all UNPROFOR patrols and is still keeping them blocked. It was requested from the Dutch Battalion commander that this area be immediately visited by the UNPROFOR commander for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the representatives of the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the 2nd Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. Please slow down, Mr. Tolimir. Too fast again. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for the warning. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you, General, follow the situation and do you now understand and realise that UNPROFOR's movements was indeed restricted as is reported here by Naser Oric, commander of the BiH army, not of the VRS, mind you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now this is about document drafted in Sarajevo a month before I arrived regarding an event that took place a month before I arrived in Sarajevo. I know nothing about this, and during my period as Chief of Staff, nothing was reported to me indicating restrictions of UNPROFOR movement within the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. During your term in office as the chief of UNPROFOR staff, was there a ban on the movement of UNPROFOR throughout the Podgaj sector? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat the answer I just gave. During my period as Chief of Staff, nothing was reported to me regarding any restrictions on the movements of UNPROFOR within the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Is it possible that you were not informed about the activities in that zone, although your commanders knew that there was a ban on their movement and they say that that had been ordered to them by the superior command, and we'll show you where that was ordered. Is it possible that at your level you did not know that there was a restriction on the movement of your troops in Srebrenica and the so-called Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to answer that theoretically anything is possible, but this is highly improbable unless it concerns an agreement reached before I entered office here and others were aware of it. But I was never told anything about this and I would find it particularly strange if such an agreement existed and my predecessor didn't tell me about it when the position was transferred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On page 3411, the deputy battalion commander speaks about that and he said that he had received an order from his superior command not to move through that area. He testified here before this Court. Let's not go over the same ground and repeat things that are already known by the Trial Chamber. I'm just asking you whether it is possible that you, yourself, were not informed that your unit was not allowed to move through the Podgaj sector area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you for the third time that I was not aware of this and that I think it's highly improbable that an agreement existed that I didn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's not waste any more time on the event that you're not familiar with. The Trial Chamber was informed about all that by a witness who had been an eye-witness to the events. Thank you. Thank you. Was Gorazde also under your control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gorazde was part of the Sarajevo sector and was certainly under UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that UNPROFOR was blocked or restricted in their movement in Gorazde as well by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any restriction of movement by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that General Smith wrote to General Rasim Delic on the 5th of June, 1995, he sent him a letter dealing with relations between UNPROFOR and Muslim forces. The document number is 1D187. After you've had a look at the document, could you please tell us what you know about that. Thank you. Please look at the last paragraph. I will base my questions on that paragraph. Do you know that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina requested from UNPROFOR command to co-operate with the Muslim forces against the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this. Could you perhaps repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There were two questions actually. The first one was this: Were UNPROFOR forces in Gorazde blocked by Muslims? And the second question was this: Did the Muslims requested from UNPROFOR command, more specifically, from General Smith, to co-operate with the Muslim forces against the Army of Republika Srpska? In order to make things easier, look at the last sentence -- last paragraph, the last sentence, where General Smith says: "Some observation posts in the Gorazde sector are currently occupied by members of the BiH army." And that's in respect of the first question. And the second question where General Smith says in the last sentence: "However" -- or the penultimate sentence where he says: "However, I remain" -- where it says: "... we cannot co-operate actively with the BiH army forces." That's the penultimate sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question Mr. Tolimir put to you to remind you are the following: Were UNPROFOR forces in Gorazde blocked by Muslims? And the second question: Did the Muslims requested from UNPROFOR command to co-operate with the Muslim forces against the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I heard and understood your question. I don't remember that observation posts in Gorazde were impeded in their duties by BiH troops, but when I read this text by General Smith that must have been the case and perhaps my memory doesn't serve me well here. In this letter General Smith indicates clearly that it's not possible that UNPROFOR is working with one of the parties against one of the other parties. And apparently such a request was presented to him, but I don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did General Smith inform you about those requests? Were you aware of those letters? Did you participate in any of these events? You told us yesterday that one of your tasks was to prepare all the documents and materials for General Smith. So was one of your tasks to look into that matter as well?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS NICOLAI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course we prepared many letters and reports for General Smith, but that does not mean that General Smith couldn't write a letter himself. And I've told you, I don't remember this letter.
